item.title: Former U.N. human rights chief Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
OSLO, Norway (AP) — Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza , won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack. Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , who have both rejected the findings of the U.N. commission she led on Gaza . The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court. Pillay has worked at both. Hours after the award was announced in Norway, the Trump administration imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal that the U.S. believes has become politicized and attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges. On the 125th anniversary of the prize's inception, the Norwegian Nobel Committee sought "to remind the world that the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts nonviolently. Peace requires justice," committee Chairman Jørgen Watne Frydnes said. Judges “guard the thin red line between order and chaos,” and the world needs jurists "of courage, vision and determination, qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench.” In places such as Israel and in apartheid-era South Africa, she and peers took on some of the world’s most painful and sensitive legal issues and most vulnerable populations. Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, where the trials of Nazi war criminals helped lay the foundations of international law. She was in the same room where the trials were held when the prize was announced in Norway. She said efforts to weaken international criminal justice “endanger the progress painstakingly made since Nuremberg, and they risk returning us to a world in which power, rather than law, determines whose suffering matters.” Winner led investigation that determined Israel committed genocide in Gaza Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which was created by the U.N.-backed Human Rights Council. The commission a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza. Gaza was among Pillay’s first comments Friday after hearing she had won. “What’s happening there is genocide,” she said in Germany, to more applause. The commission last year also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former defense minister "have incited the commission of genocide.” Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations. Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of antisemitism or turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel. Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack. In an interview with The Associated Press last year, she recalled how she worked closely with some Jewish lawyers in the fight against apartheid in her native South Africa and was invited to Israel as the U.N. rights chief from 2008 to 2014. Growing up under the harsh system of segregation influenced Pillay's interest in human rights and the law. Starting with Mandela’s presidency, South Africa’s government has openly compared the situation faced by nonwhite people during apartheid to the Palestinians’ plight. “We know too well that our freedom is incomplete without the freedom of the Palestinians,” Mandela said soon after apartheid ended. The Nobel announcement came at another critical time for Gaza, just two days after the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people and sparked the war. Over 74,000 Palestinians have since been killed, with their territory devastated . Saturday marks a year since a fragile ceasefire took effect, while Israeli strikes continue. Netanyahu wrote on X that the Nobel committee “has lost its moral compass” by awarding its highest honor to "a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state.” The award was announced less than three weeks before Israel’s election, in which Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power. Her win puts the focus on a court under pressure from Trump Pillay’s win and new U.S. sanctions bring renewed attention to Trump’s ongoing feud with the International Criminal Court, where Pillay was a judge from 2003 to 2008. In a video address, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration would “ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us.” The Nobel Committee did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment following Rubio’s announcement. Pillay currently serves as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, the highest court of the United Nations, in the ongoing genocide case against Myanmar. When countries do not have a national on the court’s permanent, 15-judge panel, they can appoint an expert of their choice. Gambia, which launched the proceedings in 2019, selected Pillay when the country accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority group . As a young lawyer in apartheid South Africa, part of Pillay’s work involved establishing key rights for political prisoners being held on Robben Island, which included Mandela, who later won the Nobel Peace Prize. After apartheid ended, then-South African President Mandela appointed Pillay to be the country’s first non-white woman to serve as a High Court judge. Venezuelan opposition leader won last year Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation. Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: The Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred. In Trump’s second term, he has been outspoken about his desire for the Nobel, but has expressed doubts that the committee would ever award him the prize. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. The peace prize follows a week of Nobel announcements Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week, in the categories of medicine , physics , chemistry and literature. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization. ___ Dazio reported from Berlin, and Keaten reported from Geneva. Associated Press journalists Gerald Imray in Cape Town, South Africa; Ali Swenson in New York; Cara Anna in Jerusalem; Molly Quell and Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; and Mark Lewis in Stavanger, Norway, contributed to this report. ___ AP Nobel Prizes: https://apnews.com/hub/nobel-prizes ___ This story has been corrected to reflect that this is the 125th anniversary of the peace prize’s inception, not the 125th prize. item.title: Pentagon to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter who killed 13 people
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad will be livestreamed to the public, the Pentagon said Thursday. The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009. On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice, "He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be. We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Pentagon officials clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed, the Associated Press said. The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961 and has not used a firing squad to execute a service member since World War II. Hegseth's comments have put further spotlight on how the death penalty is carried out in the U.S., following the failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. The failed execution prompted Tennessee's governor to halt further executions this year and order a third-party review. Asked whether the failed execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump called it "an interesting situation." He told reporters in Denton, Texas, that carrying out lethal injections "shouldn't be very difficult." Hasan was convicted in a 2013 court-martial of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and was sentenced to death. He exhausted his regular appeals in 2025. He could choose to challenge his execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution beyond the current administration. Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, told the AP that livestreaming an execution "could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it's happening." Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor, told CBS News that the plan "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally." He said, "There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media. I think it's an acknowledgment of the gravity of the penalty to be imposed." The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights told the AFP news agency, "The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture." Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 on Nov. 5, 2009 after walking into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center, at Fort Hood near Killeen, Texas, where soldiers were undergoing medical checkups. Witnesses said Hasan shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — before opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun. According to the Associated Press , Hasan said he carried out the shooting to stop soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He represented himself at his 2013 court-martial and mounted little defense, telling jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides." Why a firing squad rather than lethal injection? The Pentagon did not explain why Hasan would be executed by firing squad rather than lethal injection, the method specified in the military's current execution regulations. It also did not say whether those regulations would need to change. The Army adopted a plan in February for carrying out military executions at the federal government's execution facility in Terre Haute, Ind., ABC News reported in June. Known as Operation Resolute Justice, the plan calls for condemned service members to be transferred there from the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and for the Army to coordinate with the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Army is to be ready to carry out an execution no sooner than 60 days and within 150 days of presidential approval. ABC's report did not specify an execution method. The Justice Department separately directed the Bureau of Prisons in April to expand its protocol for federal civilian executions to include methods beyond lethal injection, including firing squads. That change does not apply to military executions. Firing squads have also recently returned at the state level. Five states allow them, according to the Death Penalty Information Center : Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho made the firing squad its primary execution method on July 1 after a law signed in 2025 took effect. South Carolina carried out three firing squad executions in 2025, the first uses of the method in the U.S. since 2010. Condemned prisoners there can choose among authorized execution methods. Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice, said, "Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner. I don't think that's what's motivating this. There's a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the 'lethality culture.'" After Pike's failed execution, several top Republicans in Tennessee said they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, told the AP , "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully." Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session. "We want to broaden it, include more methods," Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point." How common are military executions? Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions are even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan. President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge put it on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth. The last person executed under the military justice system was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl. item.title: 'Trust fund kid' vs. 'bigot': Personal attacks dominate Georgia Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The first debate for Georgia Senate on Thursday evening quickly devolved into a string of personal attacks and campaign talking points as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) wrestle for voters’ support in the closely-watched midterm race. The incumbent Democrat has maintained a lead over his GOP challenger in recent polling, but Republicans are still holding out hope to flip this seat in November. The candidates faced questions during the Atlanta News First debate in Atlanta about their stance on a range of issues, including artificial intelligence, border security, rural health care and agriculture. Repeatedly, Collins and Ossoff used their allotted time to criticize each other's family backgrounds and argue that their opponent was not fit to represent Georgia on Capitol Hill. Here are four takeaways from their first face off: Ossoff slams ‘bigot’ Collins The Democratic incumbent referred to Collins several times on Thursday evening as “the bigot congressman,” an insult he has repeatedly invoked on the campaign trail. Ossoff pointed to the lawmaker’s past controversial social media posts, including a sharing a video from the University of Mississippi in 2024 in which a Black woman is surrounded by white students who are mimicking ape-like motions and making monkey sounds. Collins captioned the post, “Ole Miss taking care of business.” “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said in reference to the post. The senator also accused the Republican of promoting “Neo-Nazi propaganda,” pointing to social media posts made by his son-in-law and a former staffer. “It’s not just that you hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted Neo-Nazi content online. It’s that you’re robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors,” Ossoff said during his response to a question about data centers. Collins responded to a moderator question about his son-in-law’s posts, saying he “condemned racism, anti-Semitism, hate.” “I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that too. It’s wrong,” he said. Collins attacks Democrat as ‘trust fund kid’ The Republican nominee called his opponent a “trust fund kid," arguing he's unable to understand the affordability issues faced by people in the state. Collins reupped this criticism in response to a debate question about financial troubles facing rural hospitals in the state. “You know the problem is, and Jon Ossoff won’t understand this because he doesn’t have to worry about health care,” he said. “He doesn’t have to worry about trying to buy health care insurance for his family. He never will.” Ossoff hit back, claiming his opponent “inherited a seat in Congress” during his closing statement. The Republican's father is Mac Collins, the late Georgia lawmaker who served 12 years in the House. Affordability concerns loom large Collins and Ossoff hit one another over their legislative record on affordability, as rising costs of living across the country remain top of mind for voters ahead of Election Day. The Democrat pointed to rising diesel and fertilizer costs amid the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariffs. “As we speak right now, it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of the Mike Collins-Donald Trump tariffs,” Ossoff said. “Just like it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of these high diesel prices. The Republican nominee placed blame on last year’s government shutdown, which he and other congressional lawmakers have accused Democrats of causing. “He shut it down, y’all,” Collins said. “Right when we were trying to get that emergency money out for Hurricane Helene so that our farmers and our small communities could repair and prepare for this year’s harvest.” Collins skirts question about 2020 election Ossoff put his opponent on the spot during Thursday’s debate about his support for President Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election, including in Georgia’s Fulton County. “Mike Collins is one of the most extreme members of Congress,” the Democrat said. “He’s a Trump puppet election denier. I want to hear if Mike still believes the 2020 election was stolen. What do you say, Mike?” Ossoff turned to face his opponent, who stared down at his notes before a moderator asked him a new question about The Laken Riley Act he introduced. item.title: After pledging swift results, Trump team prepares for long economic war with Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As the Trump administration pivoted to economic pressure instead of military force to push Tehran back into talks, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pledged swift damage to Iran’s economy. All Iranian airlines would be grounded worldwide by the end of September, he said last month. The country would run out of oil to sell by the end of this week. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Iran’s economy is suffering. But those pledges and timelines by the Trump administration have proved difficult to meet as it faces an Iranian government with more impetus to endure pain than to back down. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has forced oil exports to minimal levels, depriving Tehran of billions of dollars in monthly revenue. But Iran continues to sell oil that it exported during the June truce. And Tehran moves some 250,000 barrels of oil a day out of the country by land, according to Kpler, a global intelligence firm. President Donald Trump has said the economic pressure campaign, now in its second month, is intended to force Iran back to the negotiating table after the U.S. midterm elections in November, but talks remained stalled, with Iranian officials refusing to moderate their demands. At the same time, Tehran has escalated militarily against shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, hitting more than nine vessels in a single week. The strikes follow expanded U.S. operations in the area that had facilitated higher oil flows, but failed to move global energy prices. Regardless, the Trump administration thinks time is on its side, according to a senior administration official, who declined to discuss Bessent’s remarks, including the specifics of his timelines for economic pain. “You’ve really seen that time dynamic shift,” the official said, who spoke on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the administration. While Iran was able to weather previous rounds of economic pressure by dipping into its oil revenue, the U.S. blockade removes that wiggle room and is increasing the effectiveness of sanctions, the official said. The airlines The Trump administration announced sweeping sanctions targeting Iranian aviation on Sept. 8, threatening foreign companies that service Iran’s airlines with secondary sanctions. At the time, Bessent told CNBC that “all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world” by Sept. 23. He said the Trump administration had “seen enablers throughout the world.” “We know who they are, they know who they are, and we are putting a stop to it,” he said. But as of October, international flights to and from Iran continue, including flights to China, Iraq and Turkey. Flight-tracking firms reported that international flights in and out of Iran dropped by about half in the days following the U.S. announcement. Recent flight-tracking data from Imam Khomeini International Airport in Tehran showed flights arriving from Islamabad, Pakistan; Istanbul; Moscow and Shanghai. U.S. officials met with representatives from dozens of countries to build support ahead of the campaign’s announcement. Treasury officials visited the United Arab Emirates, Britain and Oman to discuss upcoming efforts on aviation and banking. While reaching out to allies, the Trump administration addressed concerns about how long the economic pressure campaign would take, according to the administration official. “Look, we want to see a resolution to this as quickly as possible,” he said he told U.S. allies. “The sooner they can cut off all these lifelines so that Iran knows it has nowhere else to go, the sooner we’re going to get to that resolution.” But analysts and former officials say sanctions campaigns like Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast targeting Iran can take months to years to force change. “When it comes to these economic campaigns, they are only as effective as you are willing to maintain them and enforce them, and that requires a commitment over time,” said Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury Department official and senior fellow at the Washington Institute, a think tank. The banks In his announcement of Operation Economic Outcast, Bessent called for every branch of Bank Melli, a state-owned Iranian bank, to be shuttered. “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the U.S. dollar system. The clock is ticking,” he said. Last month, the Treasury imposed sanctions on the manager of an Emirati branch of the bank, and days later the United Arab Emirates blocked all branches there from processing transactions in and out of Iran. In an indication that action against financial institutions could soon escalate, the Treasury Department issued an alert Monday that foreign financial institutions could now be subject to secondary sanctions without advance notice. Other banks targeted include an Emirati branch of an Egyptian bank and Russia’s second-largest financial institution, VTB Bank. There’s been an increase in interest in sanctions compliance “from across the globe,” said Cari Stinebower, a former Treasury official who advises companies on such matters for the Washington-headquartered law firm Steptoe. “Some of that comes from the messaging from the White House, which is that the pressure on Iran is growing and will continue to grow,” she said. “I don’t see this administration as backing down or losing interest.” The blockade The United States reimposed its blockade on Iran in July after an interim deal to end the war fell apart. Since then, the operation has forced Iranian oil exports to low levels and deprived Tehran of billions of dollars in critical state revenue. Iran has continued to sell oil that it had previously exported. Iran rushed more than 60 million barrels of oil out of its ports during the interim peace deal from mid-June to mid-July, and had steadily sold some of that stock, according to tallies compiled by oil analysts. While it’s unclear how much is left, unsold, some oil analysts estimated that 30 million barrels remained last month and that Iran was selling around 500,000 barrels a day. Reuters reported Thursday that Iran’s stock of oil on vessels outside the blockade remained at some 20 million barrels. The economic pressure, on the heels of a punishing military campaign, has plunged Iran into greater isolation than the country has experienced in decades. Richard Nephew, who served as a U.S. negotiator with Iran under the Biden administration, said multiple rounds of conflict with Israel and the U.S. had already cut Iran off. “Part of the reason why they can be more aggressive on this is Iran doesn’t have as many of these connections anymore. They had already atrophied,” said Nephew. Nephew said the entities targeted so far to further isolate Tehran are “meaningful,” but “are these kill shots to the Iranian economy? Probably not.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/09/after-pledging-swift-results-trump-team-prepares-long-economic-war-with-iran/

item.title: Some of RFK Jr.'s supporters are turning against him and Trump over 'broken promises'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Once loyal to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., advocates of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have become some of his harshest critics. (Bloomberg via Getty) Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides. A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter. NBC News is first to report on the scorecard , which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives. “We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard. About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF , a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement. MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases. But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration. Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market . Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S. That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause. “What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety. White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.” “After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement. Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.” “President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement. Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with. “To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said. Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.” “I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.” Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government. Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement. “What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said. Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises. Phasing out food dyes Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration. For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however. Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?” The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines , which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods. It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.) “If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said. Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.” But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections. “The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/trump-rfk-jr-maha-promises-scorecard-pesticides-food-safety-rcna601905

item.title: Who's Eric Deters? Kim Guilfoyle reportedly asked MAGA donor to pay $100,000 AmEx bill.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Eric Deters, a former Kentucky congressional candidate and longtime ally of President Trump, has emerged in the national spotlight after an explosive report revealed his alleged text exchanges with Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, over her credit card debt. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Guilfoyle, ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and the former fiancé of Donald Trump Jr., allegedly pressed Deters to pay her $100,000 American Express balance without leaving a paper trail and, in exchange, promised to help him reach senior administration officials. Deters, 63, is a former attorney, businessman and conservative radio host who has spent years building connections within Trump’s inner circle. item.title: Public executions in the U.S. were once a community spectacle. Then they stopped.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. The stunning Pentagon announcement Thursday that the first military execution in more than 65 years will be livestreamed could change that. Allowing the world to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan face the firing squad in December would make it the first public execution since two hangings in the 1930s in Kentucky and Missouri drew crowds. In 1936, a man who reportedly confessed to the rape and murder of a woman was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a man in Missouri be hanged. Proposal harkens back to a bygone era A livestreamed execution is reminiscent of a bygone period in America's history in which public executions were seen as deterrents to crime as well as popular ceremonies, said Michael L. Radelet, professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on executions. Parents and teachers would often bring children along to teach them a lesson. The events would sometimes feature a choir, a preacher giving an “execution sermon” and the condemned, who was typically a man being hanged, giving a long speech to the crowd. In an execution in Leadville, Colorado, in the late 1800s, Radelet said Cyrus Minich, who was being put to death, told the crowd, “Therefore I apologize and I’m ready to go. Goodbye, goodbye.” The crowd reportedly responded: “Goodbye Cy, goodbye Cy.” “This is in the days before TV, so not much going on often in big cities, certainly in rural areas, too, so they were there just for the spectacle,” Radelet said, adding that sometimes it would draw a crowd because the person was so hated. Thousands watched country's last public execution The 1936 hanging in Kentucky of Rainey Bethea is often considered the last public execution in the country, said Radelet. Bethea was a Black man who reportedly confessed to the rape and killing of a 70-year-old white woman, but was never charged with murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thousands of people attended the event, which was held in a parking lot so the courthouse lawn wouldn’t be damaged by the crowd, according to the center. But there was also one the following year in which Roscoe “Red” Jackson in Missouri was hanged. The Los Angeles Times reported that some people were given passes to watch, while others climbed trees or cut peepholes to catch a glimpse of the morning execution. States started to change the policy as an increasing number of people witnessed botched hangings and as broader concerns grew over the events, Radelet said. “Instead of promoting the sanctity of life and how solemn the circumstance was, with people applauding and having a carnival-like atmosphere, that really turned people off," he said. Oklahoma City bomber's execution was on CCTV Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said they have no record of any execution being livestreamed. The closest came in 2001, when Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed at a federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana. Then-U.S. Attorney General John Ashcroft announced that victims could attend in person or view it through a closed-circuit television But will the Army's announcement about livestreaming the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding many others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood , change the situation? Maher said she sees Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments as “simply aspirational.” “There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public,” she said in a statement. Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said. Execution would raise both legal and social questions Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said the announcement raises many legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle. “This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision. Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when a botched execution in Tennessee has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes. “I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said. item.title: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Abdul El-Sayed, left, and Mike Rogers during a televised debate Thursday. (Paul Sancya / AP) GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity. Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs. Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids and NewsNation, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks. “I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point. Mike Rogers responds to El-Sayed. (Paul Sancya / AP) Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election. Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist. The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly . “I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.” Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise. “It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.” Paul Sancya / AP At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.” Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump. New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war . “I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.” El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households. “Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.” El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.” The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.” “I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.” El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer. “I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.” The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts , with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game. Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith . Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed . And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.” Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name. “Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.” He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/sparks-fly-abdul-el-sayed-mike-rogers-first-michigan-senate-debate-rcna599866

But all eyes were on trillionaire SpaceX and Tesla boss Musk following his acrimonious departure from Trump's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year. Along with Musk, Google co-founder Sergei Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD chief Lisa Su all received the National Medal of Science from Trump during the ceremony. Computer mogul Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella got the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, also the top US award in its field. Trump and Musk gave an amiable if awkward performance on Thursday, with president patting the tycoon on the back and giving him a wooden case containing his medal. Trump's uncle, who died in 1983, is a familiar character in Trump's speeches. item.description:

Former president Barack Obama expressed surprise at Democrats' expanding midterm map at a private fundraiser Wednesday night, but warned donors not to get complacent about the party's chances, according to excerpts provided to The Washington Post. "There are states right now in play that I would not have imagined being in play," Obama told donors in a fireside chat in Great Falls, Virginia, with Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware), a vice chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. "If you had told me, and - I know I'm the hope guy - but if you had told me that the polling currently shows James Talarico ahead of Ken Paxton ... I would have said, eh, I don't think so." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Talarico, a Democratic state legislator in Texas, is leading Paxton, the state's Republican attorney general, in most public polls. Obama also mentioned competitive Senate contests in Kansas and Nebraska, as well as Sen. Jon Ossoff's large polling lead in Georgia, as other data points he wouldn't have previously believed. But Obama cautioned the crowd that winning those races is far from a sure bet. "All these races that are showing we've got a two- or three-point lead or it's a toss-up, we could end up losing all of them by two points," he said. "It's within the margin of error." The former president has been ramping up his involvement in the midterms in recent weeks, announcing an upcoming campaign stop in Michigan for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and cutting ads supporting candidates in crucial battlegrounds. Previously, he appeared in an ad for Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and at an event for Talarico. The fundraiser for the Senate Democrats' campaign arm raised $3.6 million. Republican groups hold a pronounced cash advantage over Democratic ones, driven by Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc. Obama painted a bleak picture of the state of the country and emphasized the urgency of the political moment to the donors, saying he sees a threat to democracy if the Trump administration continues on its path unchecked. He criticized the Supreme Court's failure to "hold the line" against the Trump administration and stressed the importance of a Democratic Senate to the judiciary, given federal judicial nominees require Senate approval. "If you get two more years of Trump acting with impunity, along with additional judicial appointments, so that at some point the scales may tip in the direction where he's got carte blanche, you now have a very serious danger to democracy in addition to just bad policy," Obama said. If Democrats control the Senate, it could make "an enormous difference" on who is appointed, Obama said. "I would say that the judiciary, during this moment of challenge to our democracy, has bent but not broken," Obama said. "We have seen it hold the line in some important areas. To the extent it has not, it's been the Supreme Court." Obama described a "breakdown in trust, the coarsening of the public discourse, the constant violation of norms, the way that our basic institutions, the executive branch, Congress, the courts seem to have been corrupted," as signs the country is on the wrong track. "If we found out our kids were doing some of this stuff, they would be on some serious punishment, right?" Obama said of public officials' behavior. "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said. He said it can be challenging to fashion a cohesive Democratic message with such disparate candidates, but that Democrats are united by core values shared by them all. "What I can say is that I expect Democrats to stand for treating everybody with dignity and respect," he said. Obama also listed fairness for people of different sexual orientations, equal rights between men and women, ensuring an economy that is not "rigged," and believing the government should provide every child a good education among other core values. "It's not that we don't have a North Star, but we have to be able to give our candidates the ability to tailor those core values into ways that speak and relate to the particularities of the state they're in," Obama said. "I think we're doing an excellent job." item.title: The flu sidelines James Talarico at a crucial moment in the Texas Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has been off the campaign trail, sick with the flu. (Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty) The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now. But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days. His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend. While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care. It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date. “We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.” While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation. “He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.” At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event. “I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.” Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail. “After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.” Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him. Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem. “Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.” Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election. Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence. “It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.” To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.” After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton. “He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social . It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., who said it should be one of the caucus’ “top three priorities” next year. Hegseth was reviled by the left even before the Iran war began, and since then he’s faced criticism from Republicans for his handling of the war. An impeachment vote could even be bipartisan: When the House returns after the midterms, it’ll be forced to take up a Hegseth ouster resolution filed by iconoclastic Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Prioritizing Hegseth impeachment would solve a big problem for Democrats: If they win the House, their leaders will face intense pressure from the base to show a new level of fight against Trump. Yet they’re leery of the internal divisions or appearance of overreach that a third Trump impeachment might create, and still smarting from his return to office after two impeachment votes. In public, top Democrats are accordingly circumspect on targeting Hegseth. Jeffries says Hegseth should be fired and that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything out” in their investigations. Democrats have filed impeachment articles against other Trump Cabinet officials, like Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., has also filed impeachment articles against Hegseth. Yet interviews with a half dozen Democrats pointed to Hegseth as the safest place to land. It’s not just safe-seat Democrats willing to take the plunge: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represents a Trump-won district, said she was open to the possibility. “If I were Pete Hegseth, I’d be worried. It’s certainly something that needs serious consideration, and I hear Democrats, yes, but I also hear some Republicans saying it as well. I think there’s a lot he needs to answer for,” she said. Of course, it may not be even up to Democratic leaders in the end. Impeachment politics next year could be driven by an incoming crop of progressive lawmakers who could form a sizable bloc in the caucus. Any member can force a vote on an impeachment resolution, which outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, repeatedly triggered during Trump’s first term and his current one. “Pete Hegseth should be impeached. Congress never voted for a war with Iran, and he’s been running one since February anyway. It’s cost innocent lives and more than $40 billion of our money,” said Melat Kiros, a Colorado progressive who is heavily favored to win election to the House in November. Massie’s Hegseth resolution, among other allegations, lays out charges of violating Congress’ war powers and carrying out extrajudicial killings. “They all should be impeached — President Trump and his cabinet that’s enabled him to do everything that he has right now,” said Adam Hamawy, a fellow Justice Democrats-aligned progressive from New Jersey. “Now, whether we’re going to be able to do that is another thing, but it’s not something that, you know, we should just ignore because it’s not possible.” The Pentagon defended Hegseth’s record in a statement. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way,” said Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson, adding that the Pentagon “is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before.” Know More It’s unclear if Hegseth will leave the administration post-midterms. While Trump is known to be unpredictable, he likes Hegseth a lot, and those familiar with the situation are skeptical of any looming changes at the top of the department. Still, other Democrats say they need to balance impeachment with acting on cost-of-living issues like healthcare that they believe will tip the midterms in their favor. “There’s going to have to be a balance of addressing needs and meeting our constituents where they’re at, and also part of restoring the faith of the American people in our own government and restoring the integrity of our democratic institutions — it requires holding bad actors to justice,” said Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J. The Massie resolution will be a good test for Democratic support for going after Hegseth. Some Democrats are loath to support a measure drafted by a Republican and before any kind of investigative process has been completed. But some leaders like Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Committee Democrat, have signaled they could back the Massie measure. The House has only ever impeached two Cabinet secretaries, with the most recent being the GOP-led impeachment of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. The then-Democratic Senate voted to toss the articles of impeachment. If Democrats take both the House and Senate next year, Hegseth could get a debilitating trial in the upper chamber. Nicholas’s view Taking on Hegseth is basically a free shot for Democrats. It allows them to demonstrate to the base that they could take action against the Trump administration without the risk of backlash that impeaching the president himself could bring. But they’ll only be able to keep a lid on the prospect of impeaching Trump for so long. With many in the party pushing for investigations of potential malfeasance by the administration, party leaders will face tough choices about consequences if those probes do turn up wrongdoing. And unlike 2018, when purple-district Democrats ran away from impeaching Trump, some are already embracing it. San Diego City Councilmember Marni von Wilpert, who’s running in a newly redrawn purple district, called recent comments by Trump about Iran’s ability to “take out” San Diego and Los Angeles an “impeachable offense.” Notable Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee are weighing the creation of an oversight subpanel to probe Hegseth’s department, Politico reported. item.title: The midterms could make or break these politicians' 2028 presidential ambitions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — As most of the political world focuses on next month's midterm elections , the shadow primary for the 2028 presidential contest is quietly playing out in public view. Democratic and Republican presidential prospects have been crisscrossing the country, raising money and tapping their political connections to help boost their parties' candidates — and their own White House ambitions. Here's a closer look at some of the leading prospects and how their political futures may be influenced by what happens Nov. 3. Newsom has a Southern strategy Gavin Newsom leaves the California governor's office at the end of the year, and he's been among the most active Democrats throughout the midterms. He's paid particular attention to the South, where he's campaigned with candidates up and down the ballot in states like Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina and, not surprisingly, South Carolina, which hosts the party's first presidential primary contest in 2028. The Southern focus aligns with the mission of Newsom's Campaign for Democracy political action committee, which was established in 2023 to help his party compete in red states. But it could also help endear him to African American voters, who make up the heart of the Democratic base. Newsom's star power — and his extensive email list — has strengthened his relationships with key Democratic officials in states like Nevada and New Hampshire, where he's sent out fundraising emails that have generated a surge of donations in recent months. Perhaps Newsom's biggest midterm contribution was backing Proposition 50, California's response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander. The proposition, approved by California voters last year, created a new congressional map that may allow Democrats to pick up as many as five additional U.S. House seats in California this fall. As a presidential candidate, the California governor could argue that he was on the front lines of the redistricting battle. But if Democrats do not win all five seats in his state, Newsom's message could be muffled. Vance's fate is tied to Trump No potential candidate’s fate is as closely tied to President Donald Trump and Republicans’ performance as Vice President JD Vance. The 42-year-old has embarked on an aggressive midterm campaign schedule — from the Midwest, to the South, to Alaska — and focused on the administration’s efforts to root out fraud. A key state will be Ohio, which Vance briefly represented in the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance’s seat in 2025, is facing an aggressive challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in the governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton is in a close contest with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The effectiveness of the conservative group Turning Point Action will also be scrutinized. Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point co-founder Charlie Kirk and the organization’s new leader, has already endorsed Vance’s potential presidential bid and leaders have said they intend to use the group to support his campaign. Vance has said he is not focused on running for president, but “trying to help elect Republicans.” Shapiro is all about Pennsylvania Among the Democrats leading the 2028 conversation, none have done less beyond their home state than Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. He hasn't visited any early primary states or campaigned with any midterm candidates beyond his state. That's by design for a 53-year-old Democrat whose selling point as a presidential candidate might be his clout in Pennsylvania, which has emerged as perhaps the most important swing state in the nation. Shapiro is expected to cruise to reelection over his Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, which has allowed him to spend his political capital elsewhere. Shapiro has gone all in to ensure Democrats win both chambers of the state legislature in November, and he's devoted significant time and resources to flipping four congressional seats. If Shapiro can demonstrate strength in swing counties like Beaver, Luzerne or Erie, it could help him make a credible claim to winning back some of the working-class voters that Democrats have lost in the Trump era. Beshear faces risk and reward As chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear may have done more than any other potential candidate to boost his national profile during the midterms. He’ll headline a get-out-the-vote tour through key states, beginning with Nevada on Oct. 22. He also spent some of the campaign on a national book tour, allowing him to cozy up to influential Democrats in early states. Still, Beshear’s spending decisions as chief of the governors association in 2026 may present the highest risk and reward for him heading into 2028. He’s been active in supporting Democratic candidates in traditional swing states like Wisconsin, Michigan and Arizona while pushing into Republican-leaning states like Ohio and Iowa, places he argues could be critical in the next White House campaign. But Democrats in other states are clamoring for more resources and warning Beshear of blowback if he doesn't deliver. Under pressure, the governors association sent $1 million this week to help the candidate for Texas governor, Gina Hinojosa. Cruz hits the road Texas Sen. Ted Cruz has long been one of his party's most active campaigners and fundraisers, and he is continuing those efforts this year as he openly weighs another presidential bid. His Truth and Courage PAC has spent more than $2.4 million this year on ads supporting midterm candidates, according to AdImpact, mostly to help Senate candidate Ken Paxton in his home state. Cruz has traveled three times to Iowa, the first state on Republicans' nominating calendar and where he won the caucuses during the 2016 primary. He’ll be in Alaska next week, and is also planning trips to South Carolina, North Carolina and most likely Michigan. Pritzker's money plays Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is seeking his third term in November, but the Democrat has focused more on helping midterm candidates in other states. Pritzker's team says the billionaire Democrat has already donated $38 million to the party's midterm efforts, including personal donations and roughly $20 million through his Ready for the Fight PAC, which is focused on taking down MAGA candidates, even in long-shot districts. More than other 2028 prospects, Pritzker has been focused on the Texas governor's race, where he donated $1 million this week, on top of $200,000 he gave earlier. He's also been active on the speaker circuit, having participated in more than 75 events across the country, including in Nevada and New Hampshire. He's expected to visit South Carolina before Election Day as well. AOC's progressive politics face a test Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York has been increasingly open about a potential presidential run, where she would be a major player in the Democratic Party's progressive lane. But first, she's trying to prove that her brand of politics can succeed in a presidential swing state like Michigan, where she has thrown her weight behind Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. They appeared together this week at a New York City fundraiser, and she cast his campaign as a broader test for the progressive movement. “If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” Ocasio-Cortez told the audience. Ocasio-Cortez and other Democrats have acknowledged that she'll face questions about whether she can appeal to voters across the country. Ocasio-Cortez argues an El-Sayed victory in Michigan, which is one of the early states in the next Democratic presidential primary, could challenge some of those assumptions. Buttigieg keeps a busy schedule Since leaving his job as transportation secretary under President Joe Biden, Pete Buttigieg has had the luxury of free time. He has used it to aggressively travel across the country, raising money and campaigning for Democrats on the ballot this year. Buttigieg has endorsed nearly 100 candidates this cycle, from state legislative contests to U.S. Senate races, and has appeared on the campaign trail with roughly half of them, according to his team. He has visited 37 states since leaving office. The range of those appearances also offers a glimpse at Buttigieg’s appeal within the party. Democrats have welcomed him even in deeply Republican territory, including Nancy Lacore, a U.S. House candidate in South Carolina who campaigned with Buttigieg in August. He also helped bring Democratic candidates together for a Michigan unity event in August after hotly contested primaries. item.title: Trump's memorial arch faces new lawsuit from Arlington County, Virginia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a lawsuit Thursday opposing the construction of the Triumphal Arch, becoming the first governmental body to take legal action against President Donald Trump's planned monument. The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, criticized the speed at which the project slated for Memorial Circle has moved without going through the full review process. “The National Park Service, the agency responsible for projects on national park land such as Memorial Circle, is proceeding full-speed toward ground-disturbing construction,” the lawsuit said. “Although the agency has claimed that a final decision to construct the Arch has not yet been made and purports to be engaged in a routine decisional process, that rushed process appears to be a pretext designed to shore up justifications for building the Arch in accordance with the President’s repeated marching orders.” The lawsuit asks that “the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the arch” be halted to ensure that the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act be followed and proper analysis and testing be done. “The Arlington County Board has filed this lawsuit because our community has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project,” Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a statement. He added that the county has acted in good faith in the review process, pointing out the “severe, unique, and wide-ranging negative impacts” the project will have on the county and its residents, only to see them ignored. Memorial Circle sits on federal parkland west of the Potomac River across the Memorial Bridge and immediately adjacent to Arlington County. The county is being represented in the lawsuit by legal advocacy group Democracy Forward. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said the Trump administration and White House have been "fastidiously compliant with all procedural and legal requirements and are certain this meritless and dilatory lawsuit will be dismissed.” The arch will become one of the world's most iconic landmarks, he added. "It will enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike.” The lawsuit came a day after the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson expressed concerns that the 250-foot (76-meter) arch compounds multiple safety issues that she said have gone unaddressed since a deadly January 2025, crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump’s plan to turn the arch into “a top grade military complex” able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition. Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., saying the project needs to be approved by Congress. The judge in that lawsuit said the administration must give the court 48 hours before undertaking any activities related to or in preparation for construction of the arch. The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trumps-memorial-arch-faces-lawsuit-020649944.html
